issues.legal_issue: An accused must be informed of the incriminating circumstances relied on and given an opportunity to explain them, including material evidence added after an earlier examination.
material_facts: The trial court asked whether the accused had committed the alleged acts but did not explain the evidentiary circumstances on which it relied.
After the witness’s evidence was recorded afresh at trial, the accused was not questioned about that additional evidence.
The Court found that the accused could have given answers to the omitted matters and that the failure caused grave prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The examination of the accused was inadequate and caused grave prejudice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the court to put the relevant incriminating circumstances to the accused clearly and afford an opportunity to meet them. The Court relied on its earlier decision in Tara Singh v. The State concerning the importance of that examination.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and incriminating_circumstances_not_explained and material_additional_evidence_not_put and opportunity_to_answer_denied

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.incriminating_circumstances_not_explaine: The trial court did not explain to the accused the evidentiary circumstances it intended to rely on.
predicates.material_additional_evidence_not_put: Material evidence added after an earlier examination was not put to the accused for an answer.
predicates.opportunity_to_answer_denied: The accused was deprived of a meaningful opportunity to respond to the circumstances relied on against them.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction involves unexplained incriminating circumstances and material evidence the accused had no opportunity to answer, the accused’s examination is prejudicially inadequate.

issues.legal_issue: A committal-court deposition cannot be transferred and used as substantive evidence at trial without first making an effort to determine whether the witness is available to testify.
material_facts: The witness had testified in the committal court but was not initially called at the trial.
The trial court transferred her committal deposition and used it as substantive evidence without trying to find out whether she was available.
The High Court condemned that course and had the witness’s evidence recorded at trial.
issues.conclusion: The initial use of the committal deposition as substantive evidence without checking the witness’s availability was rightly condemned.
issues.legal_principle: Section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was invoked to transfer the deposition, but the Court approved the finding that the deposition had been wrongly used as substantive evidence without an effort to establish whether the witness could be found and examined.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.committal_deposition_used_as_substantive: A witness’s earlier deposition from committal proceedings was transferred and relied on as substantive evidence at trial.
predicates.witness_availability_not_checked: The trial court did not make an effort to determine whether the witness was available to testify.

issues.definition: At a criminal trial, using a committal deposition as substantive evidence without checking whether the witness is available is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction cannot rest on the sole testimony of an unreliable witness when the surrounding circumstances do not provide reliable corroboration.
material_facts: The conviction rested on the wife’s testimony, although she delayed disclosing the alleged killing and was not traceable for several days.

Her account did not explain what happened to another person who had accompanied the deceased, and the Court considered it possible that she was shielding that person and had a motive to implicate her husband.
The other witness who said he heard sounds of strangulation and was told of the killing did not inform anyone at the time, conduct the Court considered unnatural and inexplicable.
There was no factual corroboration of the wife’s account, and the source of the information that led to the discovery of the body was not examined.
issues.conclusion: The evidence was not reliable enough to sustain the conviction; the Court set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the evidence and surrounding circumstances as a whole and held that a conviction could not be based on evidence of this character. It cited no earlier case for this evidentiary conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and sole_incriminating_witness_unreliable and material_circumstances_undermine_account and reliable_corroboration_absent

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.sole_incriminating_witness_unreliable: The only witness directly connecting the accused to the crime gave an account whose reliability was undermined by delayed disclosure or a possible motive to implicate the accused.
predicates.material_circumstances_undermine_account: Other significant circumstances, including unexplained conduct or gaps in the account, weakened the witness’s version of events.
predicates.reliable_corroboration_absent: No reliable evidence independently corroborated the sole witness’s account.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction involves an unreliable sole incriminating witness, significant circumstances undermining that witness, and no reliable corroboration, the conviction cannot stand.
